title: Why a Swiss exporter’s invoicing currency matters for its margins
summary: Martin Schlegel’s St Gallen presentation shows how the same franc appreciation can affect two exporters differently. About half of the firms shown on slide 9 reported pressure on margins. Lower sales were another response. Roughly one in ten reported a gain through costs.

Slides 10–11 present shares of export value by sector and invoicing currency. Pharma accounted for 47% of the total shown, followed by machinery, electrical goods and metals at 24%. The dollar share was 31%, the euro share 25% and the franc share 42%. These are different breakdowns of the same exports.

questions.question: Why can margins fall before the sales price changes?
questions.detail: If a contract fixes a euro price, each euro buys fewer francs after an appreciation. Swiss payroll can stay unchanged while franc revenue per unit falls. A cheaper imported component offsets part of the loss.

questions.question: What makes the sector distribution relevant?
questions.detail: A large pharmaceutical share gives that industry substantial weight in aggregate exports. A manufacturer that competes intensely on price can face much greater pressure than the headline total suggests.

questions.question: Can the two charts identify Swiss exporters’ exposure to the dollar?
questions.detail: The shares describe billing currency and sector separately. A joint breakdown, imported-input costs, repricing terms and hedges would be needed to estimate a particular sector’s net currency exposure.

limitation: The presentation reports rounded aggregate shares and firms’ responses. It supplies neither a sector-by-currency table nor an estimate of the effect of a 1% appreciation on profits.
